report:
### Evidence Overview

**Conclusion**: Research supports the view that opening a bedroom window or door generally improves sleep quality, primarily by improving ventilation and preventing overnight carbon dioxide ($\text{CO}_2$) accumulation.

**Key Evidence**:
* **$\text{CO}_2$ Reduction and Ventilation**: Enclosed bedrooms with closed doors and windows frequently allow $\text{CO}_2$ exhaled during sleep to accumulate to high levels (often exceeding 1,000–2,500 ppm). Opening internal doors or external windows facilitates fresh air exchange, keeping $\text{CO}_2$ concentrations within recommended targets (under 800–1,000 ppm) [https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0360132323011459].
* **Sleep Efficiency and Next-Day Performance**: Controlled field-intervention studies show that lower overnight $\text{CO}_2$ levels achieved through window or door opening significantly reduce sleep latency (time to fall asleep), decrease night awakenings, increase sleep efficiency, and enhance next-day cognitive performance [https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/ina.12254, https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0360132322008605].

**Important Caveats**:
The benefits of opening an *external window* depend on local outdoor environmental conditions. If outdoor air quality is poor (high pollution or pollen), ambient noise is elevated, or outdoor temperatures are extreme, opening a window may disrupt sleep rather than improve it [https://www.archynewsy.com/air-pollution-sleep-how-clean-air-improves-rest-health/]. Under such conditions, leaving an internal bedroom door open or using mechanical ventilation provides a safer way to maintain airflow.
